options: An attacker physically disconnects a network cable
An attacker forges a DNS record to redirect a domain name
An attacker floods a server with traffic from thousands of sources
An attacker secretly positions themselves between two parties who believe they're communicating directly, intercepting the traffic
questions.explain: In a MITM attack, neither party necessarily notices anything wrong because the attacker relays the conversation while reading or altering it.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a DoS attack and a DDoS attack?
options: DDoS attacks are always less damaging than DoS attacks
A DoS attack comes from a single source; a DDoS attack comes from many sources at once, typically a botnet
There is no real difference between them
A DoS attack only targets web servers, while DDoS only targets email servers
questions.explain: Both share the goal of overwhelming a target, but the distributed nature of DDoS traffic, from many sources, is what makes it far harder to block.

questions.q: What does ARP spoofing accomplish on a local network?
options: It is identical to IP spoofing and has no practical difference
It encrypts all traffic on the local network automatically
It permanently disables every device's network card on the subnet
It falsifies Address Resolution Protocol messages to associate the attacker's MAC address with a legitimate device's IP address
questions.explain: ARP spoofing misdirects local traffic by poisoning the ARP table, which is a common way attackers set up a MITM position.

questions.q: Why is a DDoS attack harder to defend against than a DoS attack?
options: Blocking one IP address doesn't help when the flood is arriving from thousands of different, scattered sources
DDoS attacks can only be launched from inside the target's own network
There is no defense difference — both are equally easy to block
DDoS attacks never generate enough traffic to matter
questions.explain: A botnet spreads the flood across many compromised devices, so source-based blocking that stops a single-source DoS attack fails against DDoS.

questions.q: An HTTPS connection unexpectedly and silently downgrades to plain HTTP during a session. What does this most strongly indicate?
options: That the user's device has run out of available memory
That a DDoS attack has just begun
A normal, harmless server configuration change
A possible active Man-in-the-Middle attack intercepting the session
questions.explain: An unexpected HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade is a classic indicator that an attacker is actively intercepting and manipulating the connection.
